nodes.name: Concrete mixing and curing
nodes.procedure: After pre-mixing the coarse and fine aggregates for one minute, add the cement and continue dry mixing until a uniform blend is achieved. Mixing water was then introduced, followed by three minutes of wet mixing to complete the batching process. The fresh mixture was poured into 100 mm × 100 mm × 100 mm cube molds, compacted through vibration, and left to stand at room temperature for 24 h before demolding. The specimens were then transferred to a standard curing chamber maintained at a temperature of 20±2 °C and a relative humidity above 95 %, where they were cured for 28 days. To establish a one-dimensional chloride ion transport path, the cured specimens were sealed on all sides with epoxy resin, leaving only a pair of 100 mm × 100 mm opposite faces exposed.

nodes.description: Combined carbonation-chloride corrosion durability testing (10 cycles)
nodes.source_text: The initial compressive strength of GS0 was 42.83 MPa. During the carbonation and chloride erosion cycles, the strength peaked at 49.53 MPa after six cycles... At a depth of 5 mm, the pH value of GS0 drops from 9.50 after 2 erosion cycles to 8.30 after 10 cycles... mass fractions of Cl in GS0... were 1.21%

nodes.description: Combined carbonation-chloride corrosion durability testing (10 cycles)
nodes.source_text: GS50 exhibited... strength significantly rising to 50.82 MPa after six cycles... After two corrosion cycles, the surface free chloride ion concentration drops to 0.31%... After ten cycles, the chloride concentration of GS50 was 0.70%... mass fractions of Cl in GS50... were 0.86%

nodes.description: Combined carbonation-chloride corrosion durability testing (10 cycles)
nodes.source_text: when the glass sand content rises to 100%... the surface concentration to 0.35%... mass fractions of Cl in GS100 were 2.10%... cumulative porosity of GS100... to 1.56%... pH value at a depth of 5 mm drops to just 8.60 after 10 erosion cycles

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM analysis of waste glass concrete ITZ shows wide interfacial cracks in GS0, reduced crack width and promotion of carbonation products/Friedel's salt in GS50, increased harmful cracks in GS100.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 7 illustrates the microstructural evolution of waste glass concrete subjected to ten cycles of carbonation and chloride salt corrosion.

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS detects Cl characteristic peaks confirming chloride penetration; mass fractions after 10 cycles: GS0 1.21%, GS50 0.86%, GS100 2.10%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The energy-dispersive spectroscopy showed that... the mass fractions of Cl in GS0, GS50, and GS100 were 1.21%, 0.86%, and 2.10%, respectively.

properties.description: Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy peaks indicating elemental composition

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD identifies quartz, albite as primary aggregate phases, calcite and Friedel's salt as corrosion products; GS50 shows enhanced calcite peak, GS100 shows intensified Friedel's salt peak.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Quartz and albite serve as the primary constituents of the concrete aggregates, while calcite and Friedel's salt are identified as products of the corrosion process.

nodes.characterization_summary: TGA shows CaCO3 decomposition at 650-840°C in GS0; GS50 exhibits enhanced thermal stability with Friedel's salt peak shift to higher temperatures; GS100 shows increased CaCO3 mass loss.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Fig. 10, the GS0 sample exhibits significant mass loss in the 650-840°C range corresponding to the decomposition peak of CaCO3...

nodes.characterization_summary: NMR reveals gel pores (<100 nm) dominate initially, large pores (>1000 nm) increase with glass content; GS100 shows peak large pore porosity of 0.021% and cumulative porosity up to 1.56%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: With the increase of the replacement rate of glass sand, the large pores are gradually enriched, especially the peak porosity of GS100 large pores reaches 0.021%.
